note: How the shared spine's CEFR stages line up with the language-specific proficiency exams a learner might actually sit. CEFR is the backbone because the spine already speaks it (core/spine.json declares pre-A1, A1, A2, B1) and because most of the corpus's European tracks certify against it directly. Everything else maps ONTO CEFR rather than replacing it, so one level field serves every track and a 'ramp to A1' book is a filter, not a separate corpus.
provenance: Alignments are the published or widely-cited official ones where the awarding body states a CEFR correspondence, and are marked approximate where the body deliberately does not. They are recorded here, with the caveat attached, rather than hard-coded at a call site — the same reason core/chapter-policy.json exists.
note_pre_a1: pre-A1 is NOT a CEFR level. CEFR starts at A1. It is the curriculum's own label for the ramp below A1 — the greetings-and-first-words stretch this project exists to make gentle — and it is exactly the material an exam syllabus assumes you already have. Keeping it named means the ramp is measurable instead of invisible.

cefr-native.note: These awarding bodies certify against CEFR directly, so a stage IS the exam level. TORFL (Russian) publishes its own ladder (TEU/TBU/TRKI-1…) but states CEFR equivalences.

jlpt.note: The Japan Foundation does not publish an official CEFR alignment and has said the two measure different things; these are the widely-used research correspondences. N1 is often argued to reach C1 rather than sit at it. Treat as guidance, never as a claim on the certificate.

hsk.note: Hanban's own alignment for the pre-2021 six-band HSK. The 2021 HSK 3.0 redefines the bands (nine levels) and shifts the correspondence upward; this file records the six-band version the corpus's Chinese track currently targets, and should be revisited when that track passes HSK3 material.

no-standard-exam.note: Per the project owner: where a track has no widely-sat level exam, follow the CEFR syllabus of the tracks that do, as closely as the language allows. Several of these DO have exams that are not CEFR-aligned or not widely sat outside one country (Arabic ALPT/ILR; Hindi and the Indian languages have national board and Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha ladders; Persian has AMFA). Those are deliberately not mapped yet rather than mapped on a guess — an invented alignment would be worse than an honest gap.
